Pele Yoetz 345:12: (11) They said in the holy Zohar: every single word that a person utters from his mouth ascends above and pierces the heavens, and there it is examined and judged.
Pele Yoetz 345:13: (12) It is written (Psalms 34:13), “Who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good — guard your tongue from evil.” This means: whoever overcomes his inclination and guards his tongue from evil, that is, idle words, which is like wastefully discharging seed, called “evil,” he is worthy to be called “a man,” since he overcomes his inclination and does not speak when his inclination entices him. “Who desires life” means that guarding the tongue causes cleaving to God, which is the essence of life. “Who loves days to see good” refers to the World to Come. “Guard” [netzor] derives from the same root as “siege” [matzor], meaning a wall, to indicate the great guarding required.
Pele Yoetz 345:14: (13) Logic dictates that speech be sanctified, since it emerges from the heart, which is the Holy of Holies, to the mouth, which is the outer sanctuary.
Pele Yoetz 345:15: (14) The prayer of the early ones would pierce the heavens and rise higher and higher to arouse mercy, and it would be fulfilled in them (Job 22:28), “And you shall decree a matter and it shall be established for you,” because they were careful with the twenty-two letters fixed in their mouths, not to blemish them with idle conversation.
Pele Yoetz 345:16: (15) Acquiring the trait of silence requires great effort, because of the tongue's habit and its swiftness to speak, and the nearby inclination entices it with double persuasion to speak, and speech rattles within a person like a bell until he lets it out of his mouth; and whoever fulfills this trait of silence shall have it as a key to acquiring other good traits, and is assured that he shall study and fulfill.
Pele Yoetz 345:17: (16) Whoever accustoms himself to silence shall gain intention in prayer through it, and it brings him to humility and fear, when he considers that he is before the blessed Name and therefore remains silent so as not to anger Him with his words, and he shall acquire all perfection through this.
Pele Yoetz 345:18: (17) We have learned (Avot 3:13): a fence for wisdom is silence. For a Torah scholar who speaks idle words — correspondingly, words of Torah leave him.
Pele Yoetz 345:19: (18) It is written (Proverbs 10:19), “In a multitude of words transgression does not cease, but he who restrains his lips is wise.” This means that he has the understanding to speak where it is fitting to speak, and his understanding overcomes his inclination and restrains him from a place where it is not fitting to speak, for understanding is great and rules — whatever he desires, he can do.
Pele Yoetz 345:20: (19) The Holy One, blessed be He, created two doors for the mouth, the lips and the teeth, so that he close them and guard his tongue as he guards silver, gold, and jewels.
Pele Yoetz 345:21: (20) It is written (Ecclesiastes 1:8), “All words are wearisome; a man cannot speak of it,” and it is written (Deuteronomy 6:7), “And you shall speak of them” — and not of idle matters. From here our sages, of blessed memory, learned (Yoma 19b) that one who speaks idle words transgresses a negative and a positive commandment.
Pele Yoetz 345:22: And it is written (Malachi 2:17), “You have wearied the Lord with your words,” and our sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Shemot Rabbah 13:1): the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “In the creation of the world there was no weariness before Me,” as it is written (Isaiah 40:28), “He neither faints nor grows weary.” “In what am I wearied? By one who speaks idle words before Me” — this is harder than all of them; woe to the person who brings this upon the Creator of the world. And if this is said regarding idle words, how much more so regarding forbidden speech should a man tremble and shrink. And the man who is a Jew and believes the words of our sages, of blessed memory, the holy ones, that they are true and their words are true, let these matters be written and placed in his pouch as a reminder before his eyes, and let him meditate on them day by day — perhaps he can withdraw his hand and guard his mouth little by little, until he acquires the trait of silence. And a fence for this is that he take a firm resolution upon himself not to be in the company of the synagogues of the common people and those who sit at street corners, but rather clothe himself in holy garb, or associate with those who fear the Name and esteem His Name, who have regard for their own souls and their Maker's honor and speak only good — how good is their portion.
Pele Yoetz 346:1: Sheker (Falsehood) — It is written (Psalms 101:7), “He who speaks falsehood shall not be established before my eyes.” And he is among the four categories that do not receive the countenance of the Divine Presence (Sotah 42a). And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 92a): whoever lies is as though he worships idolatry, as it is written (Genesis 27:12), “And I shall be in his eyes as a deceiver [metate'a],” and it is said regarding idolatry (Jeremiah 10:15), “They are vanity, deceptive works [ta'tu'im].” And this is one of the signs of Israel, as it is written (Zephaniah 3:13), “The remnant of Israel shall not do injustice nor speak falsehood, and a deceitful tongue shall not be found in their mouth.” And whoever possesses this trait of speaking falsehood, besides transgressing what the Torah said (Exodus 23:7), “From a false matter you shall distance yourself” — and its punishment is great; go and learn that no other transgression is stated with the language of distancing as with this one. Moreover, whoever has this trait is a disgrace to man and despised among people, for even gentiles, “whose mouth speaks vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood” (Psalms 144:8), some of them are exceedingly careful not to speak falsehood, since correct reasoning sees and knows that it is an ugly, hateful, and abominable thing. And this is the punishment of the liar: that even when he tells the truth, no one listens to him, for he acquires a bad name as a liar and deceiver whose mouth speaks nothing correct. Correspondingly, whoever speaks truth acquires a good name, and if he occasionally alters it for the sake of peace and the like, his words are heeded.
Pele Yoetz 346:2: And they already said in the Midrash (Midrash Tehillim 7:12), by way of parable, that the liar marries a lame woman, and whatever he claims [about her], he marries a lame woman. And woe to a generation in whose days this has come to pass, that falsehood has become treated as permitted, especially among merchants, who hold false scales in their hands and lie in their business dealings, saying, “Such and such is the true cost,” “such and such was given to me,” and not only this, but they also swear severe oaths falsely, and think this is included in sharpness and shrewdness in knowing how to profit, and say that whoever does not do so in these generations does not earn his bread; therefore false bread is sweet to them, until, through our many sins, we have become a disgrace to our neighbors, so that the gentiles say, “It is well known that Israel does injustice and speaks falsehood, and no true word is found in their mouth” — woe to us for the desecration of the Name. And certainly whoever does these things sees no sign of blessing, and if he sees a sign of blessing for a time, since he makes riches but not by right, in the midst of his days he shall leave them (Jeremiah 17:11), and if the way of the wicked prospers, wealth shall be kept by its owner to his harm, and his end shall be a fool; in the World to Come he shall grind his teeth on gravel, and his offspring shall be seeking bread, for when forbidden money mixes with permitted money, this one comes and destroys that one, as our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the daughter of Nakdimon ben Gurion, as told in the Talmud (Ketubot 66b).
Pele Yoetz 346:3: And nearly all the falsehood merchants speak is unnecessary, for if he wished, he could say, “For such and such a price is this item; I cannot give it for less,” and that would suffice — what does a deceitful tongue give you or add to you? And when the sin is unnecessary, its punishment grows greater, as they said (Ta'anit 7a): what advantage has the master of the tongue [gossip]? And even if he thinks to profit greatly through falsehood, let him distance himself from speaking falsehood, for according to the truth and according to its severity, he loses more than he gains.
Pele Yoetz 346:4: And whoever is a man of faithfulness has abundant blessings, and even if speaking truthfully brings him to shame and humiliation, he should not refrain from speaking the truth, given the severity of the sin of falsehood and its punishment — better to be embarrassed in this world than to be shamed in the World to Come. And this trait shall bring him to do every good thing and withdraw his hand from every evil, as in the story of a man who transgressed every transgression in the world and came before a sage to instruct him in the way of repentance, and his repentance was to be exceedingly careful and distance himself from falsehood, and through this he became a complete penitent, for he withdrew his hand from every evil so as not to need falsehood, since if he did not lie he would be ashamed and humiliated. It turns out that truth is the foundation of the building — whoever holds fast to it finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man. But falsehood is bad for Heaven and bad for creatures, bad for this world and bad for the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 346:5: And our sages, of blessed memory, already warned (Sukkah 46b) that a person should not say to a child that he will do or buy something for him when his heart does not intend so, in order that they not learn falsehood. And how greatly must one stand guard over sons and students so that they not learn to lie, and even if a child does something improper, if he admits the truth, one should not strike him, but rather warn him not to return to folly; but if he lies, one should strike him hard blows for the lying — perhaps there is hope that the boy will be trained in the way of truth, and even when he grows old he shall not depart from it. And included in distancing oneself from falsehood is not to say to one's fellow, if one owes him something, “Go and come back, and tomorrow I shall give it,” but rather, if he cannot give it, let truth guide his way, and let the poor man speak supplications.
Pele Yoetz 346:6: And it is known that the evil of causing one's fellow to sin is greater than that of killing him (Bamidbar Rabbah 21:4; Tanchuma, Pinchas 3). Behold, therefore, how greatly must one be careful not to ask his fellow to tell him something one has reason to suspect is confidential to him and he does not wish to reveal, for out of shame at not wanting to say, “I cannot reveal this to you,” he may come to lie and invent another matter for him. And likewise, if he does not ask his fellow as a request for an item that he has reason to suspect his fellow does not wish to lend, and out of shame he comes to lie and say, “I have none.” Let every shrewd person act with knowledge and be a speaker of truth, not turning back for anyone's sake, and let him weigh the loss of this commandment against its reward, and the reward of a transgression against its loss (Avot, beginning of ch. 2), for it is great, and this is a great principle in the Torah.
Pele Yoetz 347:1: Shetiyah (Drinking) — The evil and disgrace of drinking is explained in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, the holy ones, and it is revealed and well known to all, and well-known matters need no proof; and we have already spoken of this above under the entry Achilah U'Shetiyah. And it is a pity that many forget, and many drink and become drunk, and especially among the poor and the elderly this evil trait is common, and they come to great disgrace and shame, besides transgressing several transgressions: neglecting prayers and blessings, blemishing the prohibition of niddah, as our sages, of blessed memory, said, increasing dispute and quarrel between a man and his wife and between a person and his fellow, and speaking disgraceful and obscene words and many other such evils. And the drinkers themselves recognize and know the evil of drinking, which consumes soul and flesh alike, and they are full of regret, only they say that their inclination overpowers them and they cannot escape and abandon their habit — but this is a false answer, for the whole world knows that whatever a man desires, he can do. And a man is praised according to his understanding, for through his understanding he shall strengthen himself to withdraw his hand from doing every evil and abandon his habit to walk in the way of the good.
Pele Yoetz 347:2: And behold, regarding the matter of drinking, the middle path is complete, for they said (Yoma 76b): if one merits, he who drinks in moderation gladdens him and he becomes a leader; if he does not merit, it stupefies him and he becomes impoverished. And Amar Rabba said (ibid.): wine and fragrances make one discerning. And it is good for a man to drink a little beer before washing for the meal, in order to exempt the water he shall drink at the table and not enter into doubtful blessings. And likewise it is good to drink wine or beer after eating fish, to rinse and clean his mouth, and likewise between cheese and meat let him drink a little wine during the meal, and especially on Shabbatot and festivals, for they said (Pesachim 109a): there is no joy except with wine. And if he is a weak man, or one whose Torah is his occupation, wine is needed for him to be healthy and strong for the service of the blessed Name, and it shall be counted as a commandment for him if he drinks moderately in a way that his mind remains clear and settled as though he had not drunk, and as soon as he sees that it has begun to rise a little to his head and confuse his mind and his speech, let him withdraw his hand entirely, like one who withdraws his hand from a deadly poison. This is the straight path, glorious to those who do it and glorious to him among men, gladdening God and men.
Pele Yoetz 347:3: However, all these measures were stated only for one whose inclination has not overpowered him and who is not habituated to the evil of drunkenness; but if he is habituated to it, it is fitting for him to fence himself in with all firmness to withdraw his hand from drinking entirely for a set period of time, letting his hand touch nothing except Kiddush, Havdalah, and the four cups [of Passover], since habit is dangerous and from a little he shall be brought to much. And just as it is a person's way to hate his enemy and seek his harm, how much more so must he hate drinking, for a man who knows the bitterness of his own soul and the great evil that drinking has caused him — and how shall he appease his Master, or what shall serve as an atoning sacrifice for him? Is it not this very affliction he shall inflict on himself by abstaining from drinking, which shall atone for him for having sinned against his soul through drinking, and it shall be accepted as atonement for him, and according to the pain is the reward.
Pele Yoetz 348:1: Shiflut (Lowliness) — We have learned a second time (Avot 4:4): Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh says, be exceedingly, exceedingly humble in spirit before every person. Go and learn the great obligation of lowliness — it was not enough to say “exceedingly” once, but he said “exceedingly, exceedingly,” and we have already spoken of this under the entries Ga'avah and Anavah. But it appears that the matter of lowliness refers to actual conduct, in the manner they said in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 88b): they sent from there [the Land of Israel], “Who is destined for the World to Come? One of humble bearing, who enters humbly and leaves humbly, who is constantly engaged in Torah, and does not take credit for himself.” And it is known that outward arousal assists inward arousal, and through conducting himself with a lowered demeanor and downcast eyes, not seeking greatness nor coveting honor, not sitting in the place of the great, and not glorying in fine garments and precious clothing, this shall remind and arouse him to be truly humble.
Pele Yoetz 348:2: However, he should not exceed the proper measure, and if he is honored in people's eyes and moves among men, he should not sit in the lowest places nor wear tattered rags and the like, for just as every good thing is best done in secret, so humility is rooted in the heart, that his spirit be broken and his heart a broken and contrite heart, knowing and recognizing his great lowliness, his limited worth, his limited comprehension, the weight of his sins, and his great shortcomings, in the service of the blessed Name, according to what a person is. And whoever displays great lowliness and much more humility than necessary according to what he is, shall be called by the name of “invalid humility,” and it shall be said of him that this is nothing but arrogance, wishing to show people the perfection of his traits, that he is perfect in everything — what is he lacking except humility? Behold, humility! It turns out that this is not humility but pride.
Pele Yoetz 348:3: And this is a great principle in every good thing — the Merciful One desires the heart — the heart is the essence, and the intention of the heart is what matters, while speech and action are secondary. And let every shrewd person act with knowledge to conceal his affairs and conduct his affairs with judgment, in such a way that he finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 349:1: Shetikah (Silence) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Megillah 18a): a word is worth a sela, silence is worth two. Since they said “a word is worth a sela,” this implies they were speaking of permitted conversation, for otherwise it would not be worth a sela but rather a loss of several selas — rather, they spoke of good words, and even so our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 3b): a person should always teach his student in a concise manner, few words with much content, not a lengthy and roundabout way, and all according to the listener's understanding. For we have learned (Avot 2:4): do not say a thing that cannot be understood, on the assumption that it will eventually be understood. And its explanation is that one should not speak in a manner so concise that it cannot be understood immediately, relying on the fact that after much study it can be understood, in the manner of writers who write concisely and conclude, and “examine well” or “it can be reconciled, examine” [terse scholarly notations]. And if the great ones did this, their reason was that it was very simple according to the breadth of their understanding, and they did not know that days would come when, through our many sins, Torah would go and diminish, and we would not know what they intended by their holy words, and it falls upon us to have regard for those lacking in knowledge and to elaborate in writing — or perhaps they did this intentionally in order to sharpen the students' minds.
Pele Yoetz 349:2: And sometimes silence is bad. And they already said in the holy Zohar that just as a person is punished for bad speech, so he is punished for good speech that he could have spoken but remained silent and did not speak — such as rebuke over sin, or being supportive of a matter of commandment, and the like. Regarding this it is said (Psalms 39:3), “I was mute with silence, I held my peace even from good, and my pain was stirred.” And King Solomon, peace be upon him, already said (Ecclesiastes 3:7), “A time to be silent and a time to speak.” But one must weigh with a scale and balances of justice before every utterance, whether it is fitting to speak or better to refrain, and act accordingly.
Pele Yoetz 350:1: Simchah (Joy) — How good and pleasant it is that Israel rejoice in its Maker, joy of a commandment, over every single commandment he performs, exulting and rejoicing more and more than one who finds abundant spoil, and especially on Shabbatot and festivals, as it is written (Isaiah 58:14), “Then you shall delight in the Lord,” and it is written (Deuteronomy 16:14), “And you shall rejoice in your festival.” And especially at the time of the service of prayer, one must rejoice greatly, as it is written (Deuteronomy 28:47), “Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and gladness of heart, out of the abundance of all things.” And its interpretation is: this means more than the abundance of all things, Heaven forbid, “and you shall serve your enemy” [instead]. And likewise regarding the recitation of Grace after Meals, they elaborated greatly in the holy Zohar on the great obligation to say it with joy and gladness of heart, to the point that they said it is fitting to eat and drink things that gladden the heart, so that one recite Grace after Meals with joy.
Pele Yoetz 350:2: And behold, all matters entrusted to the heart require the heart's help, for if a person is told to fear and he does not fear, he cannot fear; and likewise, correspondingly, if he is told not to fear and he does fear, or if he is told to grieve or not to grieve, to rejoice or not to rejoice, and the like, he cannot do the opposite of what his heart desires — only according to his understanding is a man praised, that he change his heart and lead it to where his spirit shall be, through constant pure thoughts. And it is true that these matters essentially depend on a person's deeds and the merit of his soul — accordingly shall his eyes see uprightly, and although he himself does not see, his fortune sees (Megillah 3a), spiritually, what is above, and he shall have help from the Almighty to rejoice in a time of joy and grieve in a time of grief, and to fear and love the honored and awesome Name and serve Him with a complete service as is fitting to do. But nevertheless, it is in every person's power to be helped through pure thoughts, and if he cannot do all of them, let him do at least half, back and forth, and according to the pain is the reward, and one who comes to purify himself is assisted.
Pele Yoetz 350:3: And let the living take to heart how much joy he would feel if he found abundant spoil, and all this is as nothing compared to life; and how much joy he would feel if he were saved from death to life, for all that a man has he will give for his life, and all the life of this world is vanity compared to the life of the World to Come, for they said (Avot 4:17): one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come is better than all the life of this world. And all the life of the World to Come is considered as nothing compared to doing the Creator's will, for they said (ibid.): one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come. And if a person rejoices at finding abundant spoil, how much more, doubled and redoubled, should he rejoice over Torah and Divine service and the fulfillment of the Name's commandments.
Pele Yoetz 350:4: And further let the living take to heart how precious and great it becomes for a man in whom the king delights, whom he has raised from the dust of lowliness and desired that he serve before him — his heart shall rejoice and his glory shall exult, and all the people from one end to the other shall call him happy and say, “Happy is he and happy is his portion, who has merited such great honor” — and yet in the end the king is flesh and blood like him, here today and in the grave tomorrow, and he himself is uncircumcised of heart and uncircumcised of flesh. How much more so should a man rejoice whose King is the King of the world, whose hosts are innumerable, angels and seraphim standing above Him, whose greatness is beyond investigation and without limit, and He has chosen and desired us to stand and serve before Him and bless in His Name and speak to Him face to face at all times — which He did not grant permission to the ministering angels — and He delights in us and has great satisfaction in our deeds, and “establish for us the work of our hands” and He builds His chambers in heaven, even though He has no need of us; the Holy One, blessed be He, desired to grant merit to Israel, therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments (Makkot 23b), in order to give them good reward for their toil. And let Israel now say, “What is man that You are mindful of him, and the son of man that You visit him?” (Psalms 8:5) etc., “You crown him with glory and honor; You make him rule over the works of Your hands; You have put all things under his feet” — it is impossible not to rejoice.
Pele Yoetz 350:5: And the disciples of the Ari already wrote that when saying, “Blessed is our God who created us for His glory and separated us from those who go astray and gave us a Torah of truth,” etc., and likewise when saying, “It is upon us to praise the Master of all, who has not made us like the nations of the lands,” etc., Israel should rejoice greatly, like one who was about to be burned and was saved from the burning and made a king, for there is no burning like the burning of the soul, and there is no kingship like being the servant of a great and awesome King, serving before Him. And likewise when saying, “who has chosen us from among all the nations and given us His Torah,” or when saying, “who has sanctified us with His commandments,” and such and such many things composed for us in the text of the prayers and blessings — if he deepens his understanding of them to grasp how much good, preciousness, and greatness our Father in Heaven has done for us, his heart shall rejoice and his glory shall exult over every single utterance. And likewise when saying, “Our Father, our King, King of the world,” whoever deepens his understanding shall rejoice greatly.
Pele Yoetz 350:6: And how much more, and how much more should a man rejoice over the many intellectual commandments and human pleasures — such as one who opens his shop and blesses his Maker for his benefits and kindnesses. And one who prays and asks for his needs and the like, it shall be counted as a commandment, and he gives satisfaction to his Creator and establishes reward for himself — is there a sweeter palate than this? And likewise one who eats and drinks on Shabbat and festivals, and the commandment of marital relations and the like, it shall be counted as a commandment, and he gives satisfaction to his Creator and establishes reward for himself — is there a sweeter palate than this? And even in optional matters, such as eating, drinking, sleeping, and business dealings, if he does them for the sake of Heaven, it shall be counted as a commandment and he receives reward. Over this let Israel rejoice in its Maker with abundant joy — it is impossible not to rejoice; only one must take this to heart and strengthen oneself with pure thoughts in the manner we say, “Happy is the man who heeds Your commandments and takes Your Torah and Your word to his heart.” And in what is before us, look and see: how much a man should rejoice over the abundant goodness the Name has shown Israel and sanctified us with His commandments — it shall be counted as a commandment, and he gives satisfaction to his Creator and establishes reward for himself — is there a sweeter palate than this? Happy are we, how good is our portion and how pleasant is our lot. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 39b) that the reward of a commandment is not [given] in this world; but through the reward of joy, a person eats in this world. And the greatest reward there is for joy is that one merits the attainment of wisdom and the attainment of perfection, as our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, revealed his own secret, that he merited the attainment of wondrous wisdom and the attainment of the holy spirit entirely because he was exceedingly joyful in his engagement with Torah and in fulfilling any commandment, more than one who finds abundant spoil. It turns out that the reward for the joy of a commandment is itself a commandment.
Pele Yoetz 350:7: And it is known that for every single commandment, according to the pain is the reward. So too regarding the matter of joy: the man who is bitter of soul over the events of the time, if during his engagement in Torah, prayers, blessings, and commandments, and on Shabbat, he turns his heart and forgets his sorrow and his anger and rejoices in his Maker, his reward shall be far greater than that of one who is calm and at ease. And let the Israelite man imagine, in his joy of serving the blessed Name, that he is like one who has earned a thousand thousand gold dinars, whose joy makes him forget the grief of a small coin he lost — for the joy of serving the blessed Name is greater than this compared to all the events of this world's time. And even grief of the soul, such as over the destruction of the Holy Temple and over one's sins, which one is obligated to grieve and lament over — not all times are equal, but rather there is a time for grief alone and a time for joy alone, and let no stranger intrude upon his joy.
Pele Yoetz 350:8: And a person must be master of his own spirit, to grieve when he wishes and to rejoice when he wishes, and neither should encroach upon the other's territory, but rather joy and grief should each stand in its place, so that when he wishes he brings out this one, and when he wishes he brings out that one. And sometimes he must rejoice on one side and grieve on another, with “an eye weeping bitterly and a heart rejoicing,” such as on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, as I have written in its place. And sometimes joy shall predominate and grief shall be minimal, like a passing shadow, such as on festivals when saying, “Because of our sins we were exiled from our land”; and sometimes the reverse — a matter in its proper time, how good it is. Regarding such a thing it is said (Proverbs 16:32), “Better is one slow to anger than a mighty man, and one who rules his spirit than one who conquers a city.”
Pele Yoetz 350:9: And it is not enough for a person that his own heart rejoice, but he should also gladden the heart of the wretched and downtrodden as much as he can, by honoring them, cherishing them, elevating them, and benefiting them, and it shall be counted as a great commandment. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 6b): whoever benefits from a groom's feast and does not gladden him transgresses five voices [violates several verses]. And it is fitting for everyone to strive as much as he can to gladden the groom, though every person is obligated only according to his own measure, and a little with intention for the sake of Heaven is better — not like the custom of some who increase celebrations and merriment, saying they do so for the sake of the commandment of gladdening the groom and bride, and go out of line until nothing remains in their hands but transgression, such as singing foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation, and the mixing of men and adorned women, singing and dancing together, and Satan dances among them and rejoices with them, for he has found abundant spoil — a commandment turned into a transgression, and joy turned into sorrow, Heaven forbid.
Pele Yoetz 350:10: And it is fitting for the leaders of the city to stand guard with all firmness so that people not go out of line into transgression, so that they not journey from Mitkah [“sweetness”] and encamp at Marah [“bitterness”] and Tav'erah [“burning”, a wordplay on the stations of Israel's wilderness journeys]. And these matters have a measure and proportion, as it is written (Psalms 2:11), “And rejoice with trembling” — in the place of rejoicing, there shall be trembling (Berachot 30b).
Pele Yoetz 350:11: And the great fence is: drinking according to law and in moderation, so that people be prudent and act with understanding, for if they drink and become drunk, they neither know nor understand, they walk in darkness and become soiled with filth of every kind. “Good is the man who conducts his affairs with justice” — let Israel rejoice in its Maker with joy of a commandment, and let no stranger intrude upon his joy, and let there be no portion for the Sitra Achra, and they are assured that they shall rejoice forever, with length of years, sleep, and freshness, and no evil shall befall them, and no plague shall come near their tents.
Pele Yoetz 350:12: And just as it is a commandment to rejoice with the joy of a commandment, correspondingly it is forbidden to rejoice with an optional joy, for so they said in the holy Zohar, that it is forbidden to gaze at something that causes joy, since the smoke of the burning of the Holy Temple is a covering over our eyes. And they said in the Talmud (Berachot 31a): it is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter in this world. And how much more so those who rejoice in mirth like the nations on their festival days, or those who rejoice and fill their mouths with laughter upon hearing the voice of a fool speaking many words of mockery, who sin and cause others to sin, for one who speaks and sees others laughing at his voice, his heart grows bold and he adds transgression to his sin, and many other such evil things. And our sages, of blessed memory, said that those who do these things do not move from there until some evil decree is decreed upon them, may the Merciful One save us, for in a place where they should protest for the honor of Heaven, they engage in mockery and levity. Happy is the man who has not walked, etc., and has not sat in the session of scoffers (Psalms 1:1). And it is written (Proverbs 14:23), “In all labor there is profit, but the word of the lips leads only to poverty” — only on the day the Lord made [Shabbat], when he keeps His statutes and commandments, let us exult and rejoice in it.
Pele Yoetz 351:1: Shevuah (Oath) — It is known, the statement of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Shevuot 39a), that the entire world trembled when the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exodus 20:7), and even to swear truthfully in court when compelled to swear — for according to Maimonides (Laws of Oaths, ch. 11, para. 1), this is one of the 613 commandments, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:13), “And by His Name you shall swear.” But our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bamidbar Rabbah 22:1): “The Lord your God you shall fear” — be like Abraham, Joseph, and Job, regarding whom it is said, “God-fearing.” “And Him you shall serve” — be like Moses, the servant of the Name. “And to Him you shall cling” — then “and by His Name you shall swear.” If you have all these traits, you have permission to swear by My Name; if not, you have no permission to swear by My Name even truthfully.
Pele Yoetz 351:2: From this we learn how much those who sit on seats of judgment must employ every strategy to remove the need for an oath, and who is like the wise judge who knows the resolution of the matter? And how much more so should one not administer an oath readily to just anyone, nor to one who runs after an oath, and one should not say, “What does it matter to me if he swears falsely — let the wicked man be fed and die,” for it is known that among the obligations of judges is to judge a true judgment truthfully according to their best assessment, and how much more so is it fitting to have regard for the honor of the honored and awesome Name and for the soul of our Israelite brother, that he not lose his soul by being made to swear when he is not fit to swear.
Pele Yoetz 351:3: And behold, happy are the Israelites, even the emptiest among them, that children tremble when an oath in court touches them, and they scorn money in order not to swear even truthfully — blessed are they to the Lord; but would that their hearts held this same fear regarding not swearing so many vain oaths — that is, unnecessarily, many times a day in the streets of the city and even in filthy alleyways. May the Good Name grant atonement for it, for the whole people acts in error, not knowing that this constitutes mentioning the Name in the languages of the gentiles, such as saying “God” or similar words from the languages of the nations — all this is like the Name Havayah in the holy tongue; this and that are one, both regarding mentioning the Name and regarding an oath. And there is another reason why they refrain from swearing in court: because they are threatened with intimidation and menace and are put into great dread and the like, trembling seizes them there. And the man who fears the Name should gather strength to fence himself in through penalties and the like, to abandon his bad habit of swearing in the languages of the gentiles, for it is bad and bitter. And Rabbi Ibn Ezra already wrote that if Israel had no sin other than this — swearing in vain — it would be enough to lengthen our exile and add affliction to our afflictions, Heaven forbid.
